entries.label: Calls a set of numbers qualitative
entries.description: The student treats a data set made of numbers as qualitative (anecdotal or categorical), reading the numbers as descriptions or group names because they come with a story about people, instead of recognising a set of numbers as quantitative.
entries.signal: Chooses a qualitative option (anecdotal or categorical) for a data set that is a list of numbers.

refutation.text_md: You have treated the numbers as if they were descriptions or names of groups rather than amounts. That is an easy thing to do when the numbers come with a story, such as classmates, shop visitors or a class of learners. You are right that the numbers describe people and things; the slip is letting the story decide.

The first check is on the values themselves. A data set such as the sweets in a packet, $23, 25, 22, 26, 27, 25, 21, 28$, is a set of numbers, and so it must be quantitative. Each number says how many, not which group.

The same holds for heights such as $1.70\text{ m}$ and $1.41\text{ m}$, and for counts such as $3$ questions answered correctly or $14$ SMS messages. Every value is a number, so each of these data sets is quantitative, whoever it was collected from.
Look at the values first. If the data set is a set of numbers, call it quantitative, and only then decide whether it is discrete or continuous.

entries.label: Calls a count continuous
entries.description: The student sees a data set of counts written as whole numbers (messages sent, sweets in a packet, questions answered correctly) and calls it continuous, instead of checking whether each value is a count written as an integer.
entries.signal: Chooses quantitative continuous for a data set of counts written as integers.

refutation.text_md: You were right that this data set is quantitative, because it is made of numbers. The slip comes at the next decision: calling it continuous because the numbers vary a lot or could be many different values, when the question to ask is what each number is.

Take a class asked how many SMS messages they sent yesterday, with answers such as $3$, $0$, $14$ and $30$. Each answer is a count of messages, and a count is written as an integer. There is no answer like $13.5$ messages.

The same is true of the number of sweets in a packet, $23, 25, 22$, or the number of questions answered correctly, $3, 5, 2$. Each value counts whole things and is written as an integer. A set of counts written as integers is discrete, however large or spread out the numbers are.
Next time ask: is each value a count, written as an integer? If so, the data set is quantitative discrete. Keep continuous for values that cannot be represented by integers, such as measurements.

entries.label: Calls a set of choices anecdotal because people gave them
entries.description: The student sees that the data comes from what learners say about themselves (their provider, their favourite spread) and calls it anecdotal, taking anecdotal to mean 'personal reports' rather than 'in the form of a story'.

refutation.text_md: You are right that this data is qualitative, because it is not made of numbers. The slip is in the next decision: you called it anecdotal, perhaps because the learners are telling us about themselves, and that feels like a personal account.

Who supplied the data does not decide its type. Anecdotal data takes the form of a story. Categorical data comes from a limited set of possibilities. So ask what each response looks like, not where it came from.

Try it on the cellular providers. Each learner answers with one provider name, such as Vodacom or MTN, and the same few names turn up again and again. Nobody tells a story: every answer is one of a small number of possibilities. That is categorical.
The sandwich spreads work the same way. In a list of five answers, cheese appears twice, and every answer is a single item from a limited set of fillings. Again categorical, not anecdotal.

Once you have decided the data is qualitative, ask: does each response tell a story, or is it one of a limited set of possibilities? Short answers that repeat from a small set are categorical; stories are anecdotal.

For example: 'This data cannot be written as numbers, so it is qualitative; it comes from a limited set of possibilities, so it is categorical.' For a story-like data set, swap the second part for 'it takes the form of a story, so it is anecdotal'.

entries.label: Picks one of the two middle values when there is an even number of values
entries.description: With an even number of values, the student chooses one of the two middle values as the median instead of finding the value halfway between them.
entries.signal: The answer is exactly one of the two middle values of the sorted data, and those two values are different (for 1;2;10;11;14;68;86;99 the answer 11 or 14 instead of 12.5).

refutation.text_md: You sorted the values and went looking for the middle, which is the right start. The slip is in expecting one middle value: when the number of values is even, there are **two** values in the middle, and neither one is the middle on its own.

Take the sorted set $1;2;10;11;14;68;86;99$. There are 8 values, so the middle falls between the fourth and fifth positions, where the values are $11$ and $14$. If you choose $11$, there are three values below it and four above it. If you choose $14$, there are four below and three above. Neither choice splits the data evenly.
The median lies halfway between the two middle values: $\text{median}=\frac{11+14}{2}=12.5$. Here the median is not one of the values in the set, and that is fine.
Your move: count the values. If the number is odd, take the single middle value. If it is even, take the two values in the middle, add them and divide by $2$.

For 1;2;10;11;14;68;86;99 there are 8 values, the middle falls between the fourth (11) and fifth (14) positions, and (11+14)/2 = 12.5, which is the book's answer. The below/above counts (3 and 4 for 11, 4 and 3 for 14) are correct for this tie-free example, and the closing step (odd: take the middle value; even: add the two middle values and divide by 2) is the book's method. The claim that the median here is not a member of the set is true for this data and is stated only for it. entries.label: Expects the mode to be exactly one value
entries.description: The student gives a single value as the mode even when two values appear equally often, or insists on naming a mode when no value appears more than once.
entries.signal: A single value given as the mode when two different values share the highest count (for ages in which 33 and 42 each appear twice and every other age appears once, the answer 33 alone or 42 alone).

refutation.text_md: Looking for the value that appears most often is exactly the right idea. The part to check is whether only one value can earn that name. The mode is the value that appears most often, and nothing says only one value can do that.

Think of 15 ages in which $33$ appears twice and $42$ appears twice, while every other age appears once. If you say the mode is $33$, you have left out $42$, which appears just as often. Neither has a better claim.
When two values appear equally often and more often than any other, both are modes. Here the modal ages are $33$ and $42$.
It works the other way too. If every value appears only once, as in a set of times that are all different, no value appears more than once, so there is no mode. You do not have to force one.
Your move: count how many times each value appears, find the highest count, and write down every value that reaches it. If the highest count is $1$, there is no mode.

The book's motorbike times with no repeated value have no mode 'because there is no value that occurs more than once', which is exactly what step 4 and the closing step say. The refutation argues against the error (naming only one of two tied values, or forcing a mode where none exists) rather than just restating the method. It adds nothing beyond the book. The signal covers the first half of the description, a single value given when two tie, and that is a sound diagnosis that would not misflag a student. entries.label: Gives a mode for continuous measurements
entries.description: The student picks the mass that repeats in a day's bread data and reports it as the mode, instead of saying that a mode usually cannot be computed for continuous data.
entries.signal: A particular mass written as the mode of a day's bread masses, for example 789.0 g for Monday, or a table with a mode column filled in.

refutation.text_md: You looked for the value that appears most often and called it the mode. That is what a mode is, so your method is sound. The problem is the kind of data you are applying it to.

Bread masses are continuous: a mass can be any real number, not just a few fixed values. When measurements can fall anywhere, two loaves matching exactly is usually a coincidence rather than a pattern, so a repeated value does not tell you which mass is typical. This is why the book says we can usually not compute the mode of a continuous data set.

Here is what goes wrong in practice. Among Monday's ten masses, $789.0\ \text{g}$ appears twice, so you might call it the mode. But it is the lightest mass of the day, well below Monday's mean of $800.8\ \text{g}$ and median of $801.8\ \text{g}$. Two loaves happening to match tells you nothing about where the typical loaf sits.

So for continuous data like these, do not report a mode. Write that the data are continuous, so the mode cannot be computed. Then work out the mean (add the ten masses and divide by $10$) and the median (sort the masses and take the value halfway between the two middle ones), and use those two to judge whether the loaves meet the requirement.

verdict.reason: The error is real and matches caution b03749 and the canonical step 'since the data are continuous we cannot compute the mode'. I re-solved Monday from the table: the masses sort to 789.0, 789.0, 796.2, 796.8, 801.2, 802.4, 802.4, 802.5, 808.8, 819.6. The sum is 8007.9, the mean is 800.8 and the median is 801.8, all matching the canonical solution. 789.0 appears twice and is the lightest mass of the day, so the example is true. The 'any real number' reasoning comes from the canonical text, and the final instruction (do not report a mode, use mean and median) is the book's method. It argues against the error and does not just restate the method. No question ids, page numbers, figures or review history appear. One minor imprecision: 802.4 also appears twice on Monday, and the refutation mentions only 789.0. That omission is not false and does not change the lesson.

entries.label: Expects the mean and median to agree
entries.description: The student expects the mean and median to come out the same or nearly the same, so a gap between them is taken as an arithmetic slip, or only one of the two is worked out and the other is assumed to match.

refutation.text_md: You expected the mean and the median to match, so when they differ you suspect you made a mistake, or you work out only one and assume the other would agree. That is a fair expectation for the bread data, because the two are close there. But close is not the same as equal.

The two measures find the centre in different ways. The mean adds all ten masses and divides by $10$, so every value counts by its size. The median sorts the masses and takes the value in the middle; with $10$ masses that is halfway between the two middle numbers. Two different methods will seldom give exactly the same number.

The results for the seven days show this. Thursday has a mean of $803.4\ \text{g}$ and a median of $800.8\ \text{g}$. Friday has a mean of $802.0\ \text{g}$ and a median of $804.3\ \text{g}$. On none of the seven days are the mean and median equal, and nothing has gone wrong. The book also warns that the mean and median are not always close to each other, so a difference is not a sign of an error, and one measure cannot stand in for the other.

So work out both and set them side by side. Then compare them with the requirement. For the bread, $800\ \text{g}$ with $5$ percent under and $10$ percent over gives limits of $760\ \text{g}$ and $880\ \text{g}$. Both the mean and the median sit close to $800\ \text{g}$ on every day, and every individual measurement is inside the limits, so the supplier is reliable.

verdict.reason: The error is supported by caution WE7 ('the mean and median are not always close') and by the canonical remark 'close to one another, but not quite equal'. I checked every figure against the canonical table. Thursday is 803.4 mean and 800.8 median, and Friday is 802.0 mean and 804.3 median. None of the seven days has equal mean and median. The limits are 760 g and 880 g, and every measurement lies between 776.7 and 826.0, so the conclusion that the supplier is reliable matches the canonical solution. The method is the book's: compute both, compare them with the requirement. The refutation argues against the specific error of expecting agreement and does not just restate the method. No question ids, page numbers, figures or review history appear. The entry has no signal, so signal_ok is true.

entries.label: Thinks the median does not change at all when an outlier is added
entries.description: The student has learned that the median is not pulled by outliers and takes that to mean the median stays exactly the same, so reports no change after the extreme value is included.
entries.signal: States that the median is the same (for example $156.5$ cm) before and after the extreme value is included, or says the median is not affected at all.

refutation.text_md: Part of this is right: the median hardly reacts to one extreme value. The slip is going from "hardly" to "not at all". The claim is that the median is less affected than the mean, not that it stays put.
See what adding one value does. With 10 learners the sorted list has an even number of values, so the median lies halfway between the fifth and sixth values: $\frac{156+157}{2}=156.5$ cm.

With the eleventh learner there are 11 values, an odd number, so the median is now the sixth value of the new sorted list, which is $157$ cm. The number of values changed, so the middle place moved, and the median moved with it.
The median changed by $0.5$ cm, while the mean changed by $2.3$ cm. That is small compared with the mean, but it is not zero.
To compare properly, sort the data again with the new value in it, find the middle of the new list, and write both medians and the change. Then say which measure moved less. Here it is the median.

verdict.reason: The error is a plausible over-reading of the book's remark that the median is less affected by outliers. The canonical solution answers it directly: the median changes by only 0.5 cm, not by zero. The refutation is correct and consistent with the canonical method. With 10 values the median is (156+157)/2 = 156.5, the average of the fifth and sixth values. With 11 values it is the sixth value, 157. The changes of 0.5 for the median and 2.3 for the mean match the book. It argues against the specific slip, going from "hardly" to "not at all", rather than restating the method. It names no question id, page, figure or review history, and it introduces no measure or method the book lacks. The step 3 remark that the middle place moved is true here and is a mechanical reading of the book's own step. The signal (says the median is the same, or not affected at all) fits this error and would not misdiagnose a student who correctly says "less affected".

entries.label: Puts the mode in the set, but not as the most frequent value
entries.description: The student builds a data set with the right mean and median but includes the stated mode only once, or lets two other values repeat as often as it does, as if being in the set were enough to make a value the mode.

refutation.text_md: Putting the age $2$ into your set is the right start, and your set may well have the right mean and median. But the mode is not just an age that appears in the set. It is the age that occurs most often.

Try a set with a single $2$, such as $\{1, 2, 3, 8, 11\}$. Its total is $1+2+3+8+11=25$, so the mean is $\frac{25}{5}=5$, and the middle value is $3$. But every age appears once, so nothing makes $2$ the age that occurs most often. The mode is not $2$.

The median is $3$, so $3$ sits in the third position of the ordered set. Every age after it is $3$ or more, so the only positions left for a $2$ are the first two. One $2$ is not enough for the mode to be $2$, so both of those positions must be $2$.
Take care with the last two ages as well. If $x_4$ and $x_5$ were the same age, that age would also occur twice, and then the mode would not be $2$.

So write the mode in twice: $\{2, 2, 3, x_4, x_5\}$. The mean then gives $2+2+3+x_4+x_5=25$, so $x_4+x_5=18$. Choose two different ages that add to $18$, for example $4$ and $14$, which gives $\{2, 2, 3, 4, 14\}$.

entries.label: Reads a tall column as big numbers

refutation.text_md: You are reading a tall column as meaning big numbers. That is a natural first guess, and you are right that the height tells you something about the values in that range. What it tells you is how many values are there, not how big they are.

The numbers under the columns, like $12$–$15$, say which values a range covers. The height of the column says how many of the values in the data set land in that range. A tall column is the range where most of the values are, whether those values are small or large.

For example, with $15$ learners counting their stones, a column over $12$–$15$ that is $6$ high means six learners have between $12$ and $15$ stones. It does not say that any of them has $6$ stones. All the column heights together add up to $15$, the number of learners, because each learner's value lands in exactly one column.
To count the values in a range, find its column and read its height. That number is your count.

Each range includes both numbers in its label, so $4$–$7$ holds $4$, $5$, $6$ and $7$. The next range starts at the very next whole number, so every whole number belongs to exactly one range.

Say the sorted values of a group of learners begin $1, 4, 6, 6, 6, 6, 8$, and the ranges are $0$–$3$ and $4$–$7$. The range $0$–$3$ has just the $1$, so its count is $1$. The range $4$–$7$ has the $4$ and the four $6$s, so its count is $5$. Slip the $4$ into $0$–$3$ and you would count $2$ and $4$ instead, and both columns would come out wrong.
To count a range, first write out the whole numbers it covers, for example $4, 5, 6, 7$. Then count every value in the sorted list that is one of those numbers. The edge numbers count.

entries.description: When asked what happens to the range if the smallest or largest value is removed, or when a value that is not typical of the rest is present, the student expects the range to stay the same or hardly change, forgetting that the range is built only from the largest and the smallest values.

refutation.text_md: It is natural to think that taking away one number out of many should hardly change anything, and you are right that all the other values stay exactly as they were. The catch is that the range does not use all the values: it uses only the largest and the smallest.
The range is the largest value minus the smallest value. In the set $\{1, 4, 5, 8, 6, 7, 5, 6, 7, 4, 10, 9, 10\}$ the smallest value is $1$ and the largest value is $10$, so the range is $10-1=9$.

Now take the $1$ away. The smallest value left is $4$, so the range becomes $10-4=6$. Only one number was removed, yet the range dropped from $9$ to $6$, because the number removed was one of the two numbers the range is made from.
The book calls a value that is not typical of the other values an outlier, and the $1$ here is one. An outlier has a big influence on the range: the range is very sensitive to outliers.
So when you are asked what happens if a value is removed, cross it out, find the smallest and the largest values that are left, and subtract again. Here that gives $10-4=6$.

refutation.text_md: You worked out the rank correctly and then counted to that position, which is the right instinct. The slip is that a rank is a position in the data set **after it has been sorted** from smallest to largest, and the list you are given is usually in no particular order.

Take $\{3, 5, 1, 8, 9, 12, 25, 28, 24, 30, 41, 50\}$. The rank of the lower quartile is $r=\frac{25}{100}(12-1)+1=3.75$, so it lies between the third and fourth values. Counting along the list as printed, those are $1$ and $8$, which gives $\frac{1+8}{2}=4.5$. But $1$ is the smallest number in the whole set, so it cannot be the third smallest.

The percentile formula only makes sense in sorted order. It gives rank $1$ for the minimum (the $0^{\text{th}}$ percentile) and rank $n$ for the maximum (the $100^{\text{th}}$ percentile). Those ranks only point to the smallest and largest values when the values are in order.

Sort first: $\{1, 3, 5, 8, 9, 12, 24, 25, 28, 30, 41, 50\}$. Now the third and fourth values are $5$ and $8$, and the lower quartile is $\frac{5+8}{2}=6.5$. Same rank, different values, different answer.
Make sorting your first step every time: rewrite the data from smallest to largest, check that you still have all $n$ values, and only then use the percentile formula and count along the sorted list.

entries.label: Finds the middle of the data before putting it in order
entries.description: The student finds the median and the quartiles by counting to the middle of the data in the order it is printed, instead of first writing the values from smallest to largest.

refutation.text_md: You are counting along the list to find the middle, and finding a quartile by its position is the right idea. The slip is doing that counting on the data in the order it was printed.

A quartile is the 25th, 50th or 75th percentile, and the rank from the percentile formula counts places in the ordered list. With 12 values the 25th percentile has rank $3.75$, which means between the third and fourth smallest values. In a list that is not in order, the third and fourth entries are just whatever happened to be written there.

See it go wrong with 15 timings printed in this order: $121, 137, 131, 135, 130, 128, 130, 126, 132, 127, 129, 120, 118, 125, 134$. The ranks are $4.5$ and $11.5$. In the printed order, the lower-quartile places hold $135$ and $130$, while the upper-quartile places hold $129$ and $120$. The "upper" quartile comes out smaller than the "lower" one, so $Q_3-Q_1$ would be negative. The upper quartile can never sit below the lower quartile, so that result tells you the data was not in order.

Before you count anything, write all the values in order from smallest to largest. Then use the percentile formula for the ranks, read $Q_1$ and $Q_3$ from that ordered list, and subtract: $Q_3-Q_1$. For the semi-interquartile range, halve that result. Those same 15 timings, put in order first, give an interquartile range of $6$.

entries.description: The student counts to the middle, the quarter and the three-quarter positions (and may take the first and last values as the minimum and maximum) in the data as it was GIVEN, instead of first putting the values in order from smallest to largest.
entries.signal: The median, or the average of the two middle values, is simply whatever sits in the middle of the list as it was written; the "minimum" and "maximum" are the first and last numbers written; or the five numbers do not increase from left to right (a first quartile larger than the median, say).

refutation.text_md: You counted to the middle of the list, and counting by position is the right idea: with 9 values the median is the 5th value, the first quartile is the 3rd and the third quartile is the 7th. What is missing is a step that comes before the counting: putting the data in order.

Position only means something once the values are lined up from smallest to largest. The median is the value with as many values below it as above it. The middle of a list that is still jumbled is just whichever number happened to be written there.

Try it on the florist's bouquets: $16, 14, 8, 12, 6, 5, 3, 5, 7$. The 5th value as written is $6$. But only three values are below $6$ (the $5$, $3$ and $5$) and five are above it, so $6$ is not in the middle. Put the data in order first: $3, 5, 5, 6, 7, 8, 12, 14, 16$. Now the 5th value is $7$, with four values below it and four above it. The median is $7$, not $6$.

The same trap catches the other three numbers. Read off the unordered list, the first value $16$ would be the "minimum" and the last value $7$ the "maximum", yet $3$ is in the list. The 3rd and 7th values as written, $8$ and $3$, would make the first quartile bigger than the third quartile. A five number summary has to increase from minimum to maximum, and that only happens once the data is ordered.

So make ordering your first line of working every time: write the data from smallest to largest. Then the minimum is the first value and the maximum is the last. Count along the ordered list for the median and the quartiles. With an even number of values, the median lies between the two middle values, so you take their average.

refutation.text_md: It looks like you took the number to be a quartile. That is a sensible place to look, because the box is where the quartiles live. The catch is which part of the box: a box has three vertical lines, and they do three different jobs.
The book says the box shows the interquartile range, the distance between $Q_1$ and $Q_3$. So the two ends of the box are the quartiles. The line inside the box is the one that shows the median.

Try it on a plot whose whiskers reach $15$ and $35$ and whose box runs from $22$ to $28$, with a line inside the box at $25$. The two ends of the box give $Q_1 = 22$ and $Q_3 = 28$, and the line inside gives the median, $25$. If the line at $25$ were a quartile, the median would be left with no mark on the plot at all.
Next time, look at where your number sits. If it is on an end of the box, it is a quartile. If it is on the line inside the box, between the two ends, it is the median.

entries.description: The student reads a mark in the middle of the plot as the minimum or the maximum, instead of looking to the ends of the whiskers for those two values.

refutation.text_md: It looks like you took the number to be the smallest or the largest value. The plot does show both of those, so looking for them was a sound idea. The catch is which marks they are.

The book says the lines extending outside the box, the whiskers, show where the minimum and maximum values lie. So the minimum is where the lower whisker stops, and the maximum is where the upper whisker stops.

Test it on a plot whose whiskers reach $15$ and $35$, with a line inside the box at $25$. The plot shows values below $25$, because the lower whisker goes down to $15$, and values above $25$, because the upper whisker goes up to $35$. A minimum has nothing below it and a maximum has nothing above it, so a mark in the middle of the box cannot be either one.

Before you choose minimum or maximum, check that your number sits at the outer end of a whisker. A number on a line inside the box is not at a whisker's end, so look to the box instead: its two ends are the quartiles, and the line inside it is the median.
